Series::besseli¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::besseli() const
Series Series::besseli(double order) const

The Growing Modified Bessel Family¶

besseli() evaluates the modified Bessel function of the first kind, I_order(x), elementwise. It solves

x² y'' + x y' - (x² + order²) y = 0

and is the solution that remains finite at zero for non-negative order. Unlike the oscillatory J and Y families, I_v(x) grows approximately like exp(x) / sqrt(2*pi*x) on the positive axis. It commonly represents the growing component of radial diffusion and concentration models.

Calling besseli() is identical to besseli(0.0). The explicit overload uses one finite scalar order for all elements. Integer orders obey I_-n(x) = I_n(x) and have real parity on negative arguments. A negative argument with non-integer order does not generally have a real value, so the real-valued API returns NaN for that lane.

The transform is out of place and shape preserving. Floating input produces a floating result; integral input promotes to float64. Growth is genuine: a large positive argument may overflow to positive infinity rather than being silently scaled. Use a logarithmic formulation in algorithms whose arguments can enter that regime.

Reverse Mode¶

The derivative uses the sum of adjacent orders:

d I_v(x) / dx = (I_(v-1)(x) + I_(v+1)(x)) / 2

For order zero, symmetry reduces this to I_1(x).

Examples¶

Example 1. The default order demonstrates monotone positive-axis growth.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0}).besseli());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0635, 1.2661, 2.2796, 11.3019]

Example 2. Order one is zero at the origin and grows with a different near-zero power law.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0}).besseli(1.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.2579, 0.5652, 1.5906, 9.7595]

Example 3. Integer-order parity permits negative arguments. I_0 is even and I_1 is odd.

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.besseli());
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.besseli(1.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.2661, 1.0000, 1.2661]
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.5652, 0.0000, 0.5652]

Example 4. Reverse mode for order zero returns I_1.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.besseli().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.2579, 0.5652, 1.5906]

Example 5. A scalar remains rank zero.

const auto y = pluss::make_series(0.0).besseli();
std::cout << "dim=" << y.dim() << " value=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

dim=0 value=1

See Also¶

  • besselk() supplies the decaying modified solution.

  • besselj() supplies the corresponding oscillatory family.
